final_proof:
Let the direction angle be represented in the half-open interval $(-\pi,\pi]$, as required by the displayed formula; in particular, the negative $x$-axis is assigned the angle $\pi$. We use the standard real arctangent

$$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2),$$

which is the inverse of tangent restricted to that interval.

First suppose that $\mathbf a\ne\mathbf0$, and put

$$r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}>0.$$

By definition, its direction angle is the unique $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ satisfying

$$\cos\theta=\frac{x}{r},\qquad \sin\theta=\frac{y}{r}. \tag{1}$$

Indeed, two angles with the same sine and cosine differ by an integer multiple of $2\pi$, and the half-open interval $(-\pi,\pi]$ contains exactly one representative of each congruence class modulo $2\pi$.

Assume first that $x\ne0$, and set

$$t=\arctan\left(\frac yx\right).$$

Then $-\pi/2<t<\pi/2$, $\tan t=y/x$, and $\cos t>0$. Consequently, using $1+\tan^2t=1/\cos^2t$,

$$\cos t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(y/x)^2}}=\frac{|x|}{r},$$

and hence

$$\sin t=\tan t\cos t=\frac yx\frac{|x|}{r}. \tag{2}$$

If $x>0$, then $|x|=x$, so (2) gives

$$(\cos t,\sin t)=\left(\frac{x}{r},\frac{y}{r}\right).$$

Moreover, $t\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\subset(-\pi,\pi]$. Therefore, by the uniqueness in (1),

$$\theta=t=\arctan\left(\frac yx\right).$$

Now suppose that $x<0$. Then $|x|=-x$, and (2) gives

$$(\cos t,\sin t)=\left(-\frac{x}{r},-\frac{y}{r}\right).$$

Adding or subtracting $\pi$ negates both sine and cosine, so either $t+\pi$ or $t-\pi$, according to which lies in the chosen branch, has the required coordinates in (1).

If $y\ge0$, then $y/x\le0$, so $t\in(-\pi/2,0]$. Thus

$$t+\pi\in(\pi/2,\pi],$$

and therefore

$$\theta=t+\pi=\arctan\left(\frac yx\right)+\pi.$$

This includes $y=0$, for which $t=0$ and $\theta=\pi$.

If instead $y<0$, then $y/x>0$, so $t\in(0,\pi/2)$. Hence

$$t-\pi\in(-\pi,-\pi/2),$$

and therefore

$$\theta=t-\pi=\arctan\left(\frac yx\right)-\pi.$$

It remains to consider $x=0$. If $y>0$, then $r=y$, and

$$\left(\frac{x}{r},\frac{y}{r}\right)=(0,1)=(\cos(\pi/2),\sin(\pi/2)),$$

so $\theta=\pi/2$. If $y<0$, then $r=-y$, and

$$\left(\frac{x}{r},\frac{y}{r}\right)=(0,-1)=(\cos(-\pi/2),\sin(-\pi/2)),$$

so $\theta=-\pi/2$.

Finally, if $x=y=0$, then $\mathbf a=\mathbf0$. It cannot be normalized because $r=0$, and it determines no ray from the origin: multiplying a unit vector in any direction by zero gives the same zero vector. Thus its direction is undefined.

These cases give exactly the asserted piecewise formula.
